title: Le Nozze di Figaro
note: 1.4.2: Pop-Up Video-style bubbles timed to the Met HD 2025-04-26 scene markers (697a3182-2158-59af-aff1-6f8e9f0c9a40). Generated by facts/titles-snark/mk_title.py from spec_figaro.py.

facts.text: Today’s matinee is the Met’s 528th Le Nozze di Figaro.
evidence: Le Nozze di Figaro (528)

facts.text: Host Julia Bullock debuted at the Met in 2024, in El Niño by John Adams, who calls her his muse.
evidence: She met composer John Adams, who has called her his "muse," in 2014.
performing the staged version of his oratorio El Niño at the Metropolitan Opera
in preparation for her Metropolitan Opera debut in El Niño

facts.text: Joana Mallwitz makes her Met debut with this Figaro. Her first professional conducting job came at six hours’ notice.
evidence: She made her Metropolitan Opera debut in 2025 in The Marriage of Figaro.
she made her debut professional conducting appearance there, at 6 hours' notice

facts.text: At the 1786 premiere, the audience demanded encores of five numbers. On 8 May, seven.
evidence: The applause of the audience on the first night resulted in five numbers being encored, seven on 8 May.

facts.text: Richard Eyre’s staging opened the Met’s 2014–15 season, with James Levine conducting.
evidence: Opening Night {130}, New Production
Conductor James Levine
Production Richard Eyre
the 2014–15 season opening production, Mozart's The Marriage of Figaro

facts.text: It was Mozart who picked Beaumarchais’s play. Da Ponte turned it into a libretto in six weeks.
evidence: It was Mozart who originally selected Beaumarchais's play and brought it to Da Ponte, who turned it into a libretto in six weeks

facts.text: Servant versus count: Beaumarchais’s play, with its frank class conflict, was at first banned in Vienna.
evidence: Beaumarchais's Mariage de Figaro, with its frank treatment of class conflict, was at first banned in Vienna

facts.text: Basilio’s phrase “Così fan tutte le belle” here later turned up in the overture to Mozart’s Così fan tutte.
evidence: A musical phrase from the act 1 trio of The Marriage of Figaro (where Basilio sings Così fan tutte le belle) was later reused by Mozart in the overture to his opera Così fan tutte.

facts.text: A C-major military march: the tune mimics a bugle on natural harmonics, and the horns join in.
evidence: The aria is set in C major
in the style of a military march
The melody often mimics the sound of a military bugle by concentrating on the natural harmonics
This effect is strengthened when horns are prominent several times in the orchestra.

facts.text: Mozart quoted this tune in Don Giovanni, where Leporello sighs: “Now that tune I know too well.”
evidence: Mozart later quoted his own tune, played by a stage band as part of a medley sequence, in his opera Don Giovanni (1787)
"Now that tune I know too well"

facts.text: “Porgi, amor” reuses the motif that opens Mozart’s early bassoon concerto.
evidence: Mozart also reused the motif that begins his early bassoon concerto in another aria sung by the countess, "Porgi, amor".

facts.text: Federica Lombardi, our Countess, debuted at the Met in 2019 as Donna Elvira; at Covent Garden, as this Countess.
evidence: Lombardi made her debut at the Metropolitan Opera New York as Donna Elvira in 2019.
Royal Opera House (debut in 2022 as Countess in Le nozze di Figaro)

facts.text: In 1789 Mozart replaced this aria for a new Susanna. The Met used his replacements in 1998, with Cecilia Bartoli.
evidence: Mozart replaced both arias of Susanna with new compositions
"Un moto di gioia" (replacing "Venite, inginocchiatevi" in act 2)
A notable exception was a series of performances at the Metropolitan Opera in 1998 with Cecilia Bartoli as Susanna.

facts.text: The Act II finale starts here: over 900 bars of continuous music, one of Mozart’s longest uninterrupted stretches.
evidence: The finale of act 2, lasting 20 minutes, is one of the longest uninterrupted pieces of music Mozart ever wrote.
more than 900 bars of continuous music

facts.text: Count the voices: eight of the opera’s 11 characters pile in, climaxing in a seven- and eight-voice tutti.
evidence: Eight of the opera's 11 characters appear on stage
climaxing in seven- and eight-voice tutti for acts 2 and 4

facts.text: “Dove sono” begins like the Agnus Dei of Mozart’s Coronation Mass, moved from F major to C major.
evidence: begins similarly to the Agnus Dei from Mozart's Coronation Mass, K. 317, written in 1779. While in F major and in 3/4 time in the mass, it is in C major and 2/4 time in the opera.

facts.text: Oboes and bassoons fill the Countess’s rests with expressive motifs, which she later picks up.
evidence: while oboes and bassoons fill her rests with expressive motifs which she later picks up

facts.text: Today “Dove sono” came before this sextet. Mozart’s score puts it after; two scholars argued this order is more logical.
evidence: In Mozart's score, the aria follows the sextet in act 3
it precedes the sextet
Moberly and Raeburn argued in 1965 that this is a more logical order

facts.text: The letter duet: B-flat major, 6/8, oboe and bassoon. The Countess dictates; Susanna repeats each line as she writes.
evidence: The duet is scored for oboe, bassoon, and strings. The piece is in the key of B-flat major with a time signature of 6/8
the Contessa dictates the title and the three lines of the letter and, after a pause, Susanna repeats the lines as she writes them

facts.text: In this production, the two peasant girls’ music is sung by Barbarina and Cherubino.
evidence: In this production the music of the Two Peasant Girls is sung by the artists performing the roles of Barbarina and Cherubino.

facts.text: Da Ponte swapped Figaro’s climactic speech against inherited nobility for an equally angry aria against unfaithful wives.
evidence: Da Ponte replaced Figaro's climactic speech against inherited nobility with an equally angry aria against unfaithful wives.

facts.text: Hear the two horns playing together? That’s Mozart’s joke for cuckoldry. Verdi borrowed it in Falstaff.
evidence: Mozart uses the sound of two horns playing together to represent cuckoldry in the act 4 aria "Aprite un po' quegli occhi". Verdi later used the same device in Ford's aria in Falstaff.

facts.text: Olga Kulchynska, our Susanna, learned three days ahead she’d sing the Bolshoi premiere of The Tsar’s Bride.
evidence: she was designated the third soloist for the part of Marfa in The Tsar's Bride; three days before the first performance, Kulchynska was chosen to sing the premier

facts.text: Listen for the Count’s plea, “Contessa, perdono!” Her reply: “I am kinder, and I say yes.”
evidence: ("Contessa perdono!" – "Countess, forgive me!")
"I am kinder [than you], and I say yes"
